text.p: Gillette Co.'s $7 billion marriage to Duracell International Inc. should boost sales of both the battery maker's products and the razor giant's merchandise.

"You frequently see the Sensor Excel (razor) right next to the Duracell batteries at the checkout counter," said Edward D. Jones analyst Tony Vento. The acquisition "is a great opportunity. The merchandising possibilities are tremendous."
About 70 percent of Gillette's $6.8 billion in sales last year came from overseas, while only about half of Duracell's $2.3 billion in sales were from abroad.

But Duracell is the worldwide leader in alkaline batteries, noted Bear Stearns analyst Constance Maneaty -- and the batteries run a number of products that are now considered necessities, such as pagers.
The combination of the two marketing and distribution organisations should benefit both brands.
"Gillette sells razors, and you have to buy blades. It's the same with electronic devices; you need batteries. If you don't feed these products, they don't work," she said.

Gillette makes life's basic necessities -- Oral-B toothbrushes, shampoos, deodorants, Braun appliances, Parker, PaperMate and Waterman pens -- and, of course, the razors and blades that account for the lion's share of its revenues.
But Gillette Chief Executive Alfred Zeien markets his products not as necessities, but as experiences.
"We're selling an experience -- and there's no end to improving an experience because you can't define it," Zeien said in a March interview.
In addition, Zeien said he always concentrates on having new products in the pipeline for Gillette, which is heavily into research and development.
The merge should also boost Duracell, said Salomon Brothers analyst Diana Temple, because batteries "are the type of functional product that with R&D can be improved and upgraded over time."
Moody's Investors Service analyst Joseph Chakra agreed, saying Gillette's deep pockets will provide Duracell with additional funds for R&D.
The secret to Gillette's international marketing, Zeien said, is its very basic product: the razor blade.

"In most countries, we lead with the blade business ... we don't have to create a market for blades -- it's easy to move into a pre-existing business, offer a better product and capture market share," he said. "We then bring in two or three other business and, suddenly, the blade business becomes quite profitable."
Duracell will now gain access to all kinds of international markets through the sale.

For example, in Brazil, Duracell said it sold well in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo, but has very few sales outside of the urban areas. Gillette, in contrast, is "a giant in Brazil" and its products are available even in "the smallest little kiosk up on the Amazon River," said Zeien.
